name: THE CHIMICHURRI UP AND WAIT BURGER

recipe.history:
Chimichurri is the sovereign sauce of the Argentine pampas, a vibrant, uncooked condiment of parsley, garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes, red wine vinegar, and olive oil that has been the essential companion to Argentine beef for centuries. Its origins are disputed — some historians trace the name to Basque immigrants who settled in Argentina in the 19th century, others to a corruption of an English phrase brought by British traders, and still others to the Guaraní word for a mixed condiment. What is undisputed is that chimichurri evolved alongside the asado tradition: the communal Argentine open-fire grill where massive cuts of beef, lamb, and pork are cooked low and slow over hardwood coals. The sauce's acidic vinegar base and bright herbaceous character were designed to cut through the richness of grass-fed Pampas beef, a beef renowned globally for its depth of flavor and fat marbling.

Chimichurri arrived in American restaurants not through immigration alone but through the great steak-house boom of the 1990s and early 2000s, when Argentine-style parrilla restaurants began opening in New York, Miami, and Chicago, introducing American diners to the revelation that a sauce could be simultaneously simple and complex — no cooking required, just chopping, mincing, and patience. From the fine-dining steak house it migrated downward and outward with inevitable democratic momentum, landing on burgers at upscale fast-casual restaurants by the 2010s. The logic was perfect: the same qualities that made chimichurri great on a ribeye made it extraordinary on a burger, the vinegar brightening the fat, the garlic amplifying the beef's savory notes, the parsley adding freshness that no amount of iceberg lettuce can replicate.

I came to chimichurri through my grandmother, who made a loose, garlicky version she called simply 'green sauce' that she spooned over everything from grilled chicken to scrambled eggs without apology. She was not Argentine — she had learned the recipe from a neighbor in the 1970s and adapted it to whatever was in her garden. Her parsley was always slightly too much, her garlic always slightly aggressive, and her red pepper flakes always at the threshold of too hot. It was never wrong. I made my first burger chimichurri during a backyard cookout when I was trying to impress people and ran out of ketchup, and the chimichurri was so good that no one asked for ketchup again that summer.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — that precise 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius — is an act of respect toward the animal and the craft. Beef at medium rare retains the intracellular fluids that carry flavor, the fat remains fluid and coats every fiber, and the texture is yielding without being raw. Chimichurri especially demands a medium rare patty: the acid in the vinegar interacts differently with a properly pink, juicy burger than with a cooked-through gray one. The sauce on a well-done patty tastes bright but hollow; on a medium rare patty it becomes part of a conversation, the vinegar pulling flavors from the meat while the meat's richness mellows the sauce's edge. Cook to medium rare. Rest the meat. Add the chimichurri. This is the sequence.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves, finely chopped
2 tbsp fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped (or 2 tsp dried)
2 medium ripe tomatoes, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1/2 red onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with the dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
2. Transfer dough to an oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours at room temperature until doubled.

3. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a smooth ball, pinching the seam underneath. Arrange on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes until puffy. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C).
4. Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

5. Make the chimichurri: Combine parsley, garlic, oregano, and red pepper flakes in a bowl. Stir in red wine vinegar, then slowly drizzle in olive oil while stirring. Season with salt and black pepper. Let stand at room temperature for at least 30 minutes to allow the flavors to meld. The chimichurri can be made up to 4 hours ahead.

6. Shape patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions. Season with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Shape into patties roughly 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each with your thumb.
7. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes to build a crust.

8. Flip patties. Lay a slice of Provolone on each patty. Cook an additional 2 to 3 minutes, checking internal temperature. Pull patties from heat at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
9. Toast the sliced buns cut-side down in the skillet in residual fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

10. Assemble: Spoon a generous amount of chimichurri on both cut sides of the bun. Place romaine on the bottom bun, then the patty with melted Provolone. Add tomato slices and red onion rings. Spoon additional chimichurri directly over the patty. Close the bun and serve immediately.
